strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of pixel-based model-based reinforcement learning: reconstruction objectives can neglect small, decision-relevant entities in visually complex scenes.
OC-STORM is a sensible integration of frozen Cutie object features with a STORM-style world model, including explicit spatial attention among objects and temporal dynamics modeling.

The empirical study is reasonably broad: all 26 Atari 100k games are evaluated with five seeds, six Hollow Knight bosses with three seeds, and four continuous-control Meta-World tasks are included in the appendix.

Against the matched STORM reimplementation, OC-STORM improves on 18 of 26 Atari games, raises mean human-normalized score from 114.2% to 134.8%, and substantially improves several challenging Hollow Knight tasks.
Useful ablations compare vector, mask, visual, and combined inputs; study one-shot versus six-shot annotation; compare policy architectures; and test robustness to randomly missing object features.
The paper clearly discusses important failure modes, including duplicate instances, background/layout information, and segmentation failures. The presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the main idea is to feed representations from an existing supervised video-segmentation model into an existing MBRL framework. The paper does not convincingly compare against the closest object-centric alternatives, such as FOCUS or the slot-attention STORM variant, nor against simpler pretrained-feature baselines.

The comparison with STORM does not isolate the sources of improvement. OC-STORM receives manually selected task-relevant objects, segmentation annotations, a large pretrained perception model, extra latent capacity, and a modified spatial-temporal architecture. There are no capacity-, compute-, or supervision-matched controls, and the paper provides no runtime, memory, parameter-count, or wall-clock analysis despite practical-efficiency claims.

The headline Atari gains are less decisive than suggested: median HNS improves only from 42.5% to 43.8%, OC-STORM remains below some published aggregate results, and performance degrades substantially on several games. No statistical tests or per-game uncertainty are reported in the main table.

The categorization of Atari games into those whose information is or is not object-representable appears subjective and potentially post hoc. The reported category-level result therefore provides weak evidence for the proposed causal explanation.

Hollow Knight is a valuable test environment, but the custom reward shaping, action space, wrappers, charm configuration, and proprietary game setup prevent clean comparison with prior work. Only three training seeds are used, and claims such as “best-known sample efficiency” are not adequately supported under these incompatible protocols.

The supervision protocol is underspecified. It is unclear how annotation frames are selected, whether their collection counts toward the interaction budget, how annotations initialize or update Cutie across episodes, and how much task knowledge is used to choose object identities. Full annotations and object definitions are not supplied.

The Meta-World extension covers only four described-as-randomly-selected tasks and uses results imported from another paper under potentially different implementations. Two tasks remain near zero success, so it provides limited support for broad continuous-control generalization.

The robustness experiment replaces features with independently random zeros, which does not capture structured tracking errors, identity switches, false positives, or temporally correlated failures produced by real segmentation systems.

Reproducibility is limited by the absence of a stated code release, incomplete architectural and annotation details, and the specialized Windows/Hyper-V/Hollow Knight setup. The evaluation also does not compare multiple segmentation backbones or test transfer to unseen visual conditions.

There are technical presentation errors in the stated objective: the binary cross-entropy terms in Equation 5 lack the required negative sign if the objective is minimized, and the dynamics predictor notation in Equation 4 conditions the prediction on the variable being predicted. These may be notation mistakes, but they undermine precision.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant limitation of pixel-based world models: reconstruction objectives can underweight small but control-relevant entities.
OC-STORM is conceptually straightforward, combining frozen Cutie object features with visual inputs and a spatial-temporal world model; the exposition and architecture diagrams are generally clear.
The empirical scope is broader than usual, covering all 26 Atari 100k games, several challenging Hollow Knight bosses, and four Meta-World tasks.

The Atari experiments use five seeds and compare against a reimplemented STORM baseline with an otherwise matched configuration. OC-STORM improves the aggregate mean HNS from 114.2% to 134.8% and wins on 18 of 26 games.
The paper includes useful ablations on vector versus mask representations, object-only versus visual-only inputs, annotation count, policy architecture, and simulated tracking failures.
The authors openly discuss important limitations, including failures with duplicate instances, fixed task-specific object sets, and information not naturally represented as objects.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not isolate the source of the improvements. OC-STORM receives human-selected object identities, hand-drawn masks, and features from a large pretrained vision model, whereas STORM receives only pixels. Consequently, the results do not establish that the proposed world-model architecture or object-centric dynamics are responsible for the gains; improvements could simply reflect extra supervision, pretrained features, or model capacity. Controls using comparably pretrained dense features, auxiliary object losses, ground-truth masks, and parameter- or compute-matched baselines are needed.

The central explanation about reconstruction loss is not convincingly demonstrated. The paper provides a qualitative example in which STORM reconstructions omit characters, but explicitly acknowledges that its latent state may still encode them. It does not measure object-state decoding accuracy, dynamics prediction on relevant objects, reward prediction, or imagination fidelity, so the claimed mechanism remains speculative.

Atari uncertainty is not reported in the main score table despite running five seeds, and there are no confidence intervals or statistical tests. Several gains are small, while substantial regressions occur on games such as BattleZone, Frostbite, Gopher, Hero, and Assault. The median HNS changes only from 42.5% to 43.8%, making the practical robustness of the aggregate improvement unclear.

The division of Atari games into “object-representable” and other tasks appears subjective and potentially post hoc. No operational criterion, independent labeling protocol, or preregistered grouping is given, so the favorable subgroup result is weak evidence.

The sample-efficiency framing omits important costs: manual task-specific object selection and annotation, Cutie pretraining, high-resolution Cutie inference, parameter counts, throughput, memory, and wall-clock training. Without these measurements, OC-STORM cannot fairly be described as more computationally efficient than pixel-only methods.

The Hollow Knight evidence is weak for a central benchmark: it uses a custom proprietary-game setup, only three training seeds, no uncertainty estimates, and primarily one baseline. Some metrics disagree—for God Tamer, return improves while win rate falls from 70% to 55%—yet the paper broadly claims stronger performance. Comparisons with existing Hollow Knight agents are acknowledged to be incompatible.

The Meta-World appendix evaluates only four allegedly random tasks without explaining task selection, seed counts, uncertainty methodology, or protocol compatibility with values copied from prior work. It therefore provides limited support for generalization to continuous control.

Novelty is modest. The main idea is to feed frozen features from an existing video segmentation model into a modified STORM pipeline using standard categorical-VAE and actor-critic machinery. The paper does not demonstrate a new learning principle or a sufficiently general object-discovery mechanism.

The approach assumes prior semantic knowledge of every task, a fixed number of relevant objects, and manually chosen labeled frames. It is therefore not directly applicable to unseen tasks, changing object sets, or open-world settings, despite broader language about adaptability and real-world relevance.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not provide sufficiently precise model-layer specifications, parameter counts, Cutie checkpoint/version details, annotation-selection procedures, per-task object definitions, or a clearly identified code and environment release. Reproducing the custom Windows/Hyper-V Hollow Knight setup would be especially difficult.

There are technical and presentation issues in the mathematical specification. Most notably, the termination term in Equation 5 is written as a positive log-likelihood while the overall objective is minimized, apparently reversing the binary cross-entropy sign. Several architectural and loss details are deferred or described ambiguously.

Overall, the work is plausible and experimentally promising, but the confounded comparison, insufficient statistical reporting, weak evidence for the proposed mechanism, modest novelty, and limited reproducibility leave the main claims below the standard for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically meaningful object-centric extension of STORM: decision-relevant objects are tracked with a frozen pretrained vision model, encoded separately, and modeled jointly with visual observations through spatial-temporal attention.
The empirical scope is strong. Evaluation covers all 26 Atari 100k games with five seeds, six visually complex Hollow Knight bosses with three seeds, and four continuous-control Meta-World tasks.

Results are broadly positive: OC-STORM improves over the matched STORM reimplementation on 18 of 26 Atari games, raises aggregate Atari mean HNS from 114.2% to 134.8%, and generally improves convergence and final returns on Hollow Knight.

The analysis includes useful ablations of feature vectors versus masks, object-only versus combined visual input, attention- versus MLP-based policies, annotation count, and simulated tracking failures. These support several important design decisions.

The custom Hollow Knight setup is a valuable contribution because it tests pixel-based agents in substantially richer scenes than standard Atari environments. The paper is clearly written and candidly discusses failures involving duplicate objects and background information.
weaknesses: The method requires users to identify task-relevant object categories, choose a fixed object count, and provide task-specific masks. This supplies strong semantic prior knowledge and limits the claimed generality and autonomy; transfer to new tasks without renewed annotation is not evaluated.

The main Atari evidence lacks confidence intervals or statistical tests. Per-game conclusions and the statement that the method wins on 18 games are based on mean scores despite high variance typical of deep RL. The object-representable partition in Table 2 also appears manually determined after observing the tasks and needs a preregistered or objective criterion.

The matched baseline controls the basic STORM configuration but not model capacity or total computation. OC-STORM adds a high-resolution Cutie pass and extra object encoders, latents, and attention computation. Parameter-matched baselines and training/inference throughput or wall-clock measurements are needed to distinguish representational benefits from additional capacity and quantify practical cost.

Novelty is moderate: the central idea is an effective integration of a pretrained semi-supervised tracker with an existing world-model algorithm, while most individual architectural and optimization components are standard. Comparisons with other object-centric world models are limited, particularly on shared benchmarks.

The Hollow Knight benchmark is custom and difficult to reproduce, relying on a commercial game, a Windows virtual machine, a modding plugin, hand-crafted rewards, chosen charms, and task-specific annotations. The submission does not provide sufficiently concrete artifact-release information to establish reproducibility.

The Meta-World study does not state the number of seeds or show uncertainty, and the four tasks are described as randomly selected without a reproducible selection procedure. The qualitative reconstruction experiment likewise does not quantitatively establish that object features preserve all control-relevant information.

There is an apparent sign error in Equation 5: the termination log-likelihood is added to a loss being minimized rather than negated. This is likely a presentation error given the reported results, but it should be corrected or reconciled with the implementation.

strengths: OC-STORM presents a clear and practically relevant idea: augmenting pixel-based world models with compact object features from few-shot-prompted, frozen video segmentation models. The spatial-temporal architecture provides a sensible mechanism for modeling object interactions and dynamics.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering all 26 Atari 100k games, six Hollow Knight bosses, four Meta-World tasks, two world-model backbones, two segmentation models, and vector- versus mask-based representations.

Results consistently support the main empirical hypothesis. On Atari, Cutie-OC improves STORM from 107.2% to 134.8% mean HNS and from 35.5% to 43.8% median HNS; improvement is also observed with DreamerV3. Hollow Knight results show particularly substantial gains on difficult bosses such as Mage Lord and Pure Vessel.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses of object-only inputs, missing objects, annotation count, simulated tracking failures, policy architecture, feature completeness, and computational overhead. Five-seed Atari experiments and three-seed Hollow Knight experiments are stronger than common minimal evaluations.

The manuscript is clearly organized, provides architectural and optimization details, documents the custom Hollow Knight setup, and candidly discusses failure modes involving duplicate objects and geometric structures.
weaknesses: The core attribution is not fully isolated. OC-STORM adds a large pretrained vision model, extra object encoders and tokens, spatial attention, and task-specific human object selection simultaneously. There is no parameter- or representation-matched baseline using generic pretrained visual features, object coordinates, or equivalent additional model capacity, so the results do not establish that object-centric structure itself causes the gains.

Claims of statistical significance are unsupported: Atari tables provide no variance, confidence intervals, or paired tests, while several per-game improvements are modest or inconsistent. Hollow Knight uses only three training seeds, and OC-STORM has a lower win rate than STORM on God Tamer despite a higher return.

The 'object-detectable' Atari partition is subjective and apparently determined after inspecting segmentation behavior. Reporting much larger gains on this post hoc subset risks selection bias unless the classification criterion is formalized and fixed independently of agent outcomes.

The claimed state of the art on Hollow Knight is difficult to substantiate because this is a custom, nonstandard benchmark with author-designed reward shaping, game modifications, charm settings, and wrapper details. The paper itself acknowledges that existing comparisons are not directly comparable; against established Atari methods, OC-STORM is competitive but not state of the art overall.

The approach requires humans to know and annotate every task-relevant object, fixes the number and identity of objects per environment, and uses six annotations per Atari game or twelve per Hollow Knight boss. Annotation time, sensitivity to annotator choice, transfer of annotations across levels or tasks, and performance when relevant objects are omitted are not sufficiently quantified under the full pixel-plus-object model.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the project-page field is blank, no implementation or annotation dataset is identified, and several experiment details remain ambiguous, including Meta-World seed counts and uncertainty, parameter counts, preprocessing consistency, and the exact rule used to select annotation frames.

There are technical presentation errors that should be corrected. Most notably, Equation 5 adds the log-likelihood terms for termination to a loss that is minimized, rather than their negative; taken literally, this objective has the wrong sign. There are also notation and citation mistakes, such as reusing K for both object count and transformer layers and misattributing SAM2 in Section 4.1.

strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of pixel-based model-based RL: small, decision-relevant objects can be poorly represented by reconstruction-driven world models.
Using features from few-shot video-object segmentation models is practically motivated, and the spatial-temporal object/scene architecture is a reasonable integration into STORM and DreamerV3.

The experimental scope is broader than average, covering 26 Atari games, six Hollow Knight bosses, four Meta-World tasks, two world-model backbones, two segmentation models, and vector- versus mask-based representations.
Several useful analyses are included, such as annotation-count sensitivity, missing-object ablations, simulated feature dropout, runtime measurements, and object-feature reconstruction.
weaknesses: The principal Atari comparison does not isolate the proposed object-centric mechanism. OC-STORM receives manually selected object identities, annotated masks, high-resolution inputs, pretrained Cutie features, additional latent tokens, and greater model capacity and compute, while the STORM baseline does not. Capacity-matched controls and simpler supervised baselines such as masked crops, coordinates, bounding boxes, or generic pretrained visual features are missing.

The claimed state-of-the-art sample efficiency is unsupported. On the paper's own Atari table, OC-STORM is below DIAMOND in mean human-normalized score and below Delta-IRIS in median score. The Hollow Knight benchmark is custom and not directly comparable to prior work, so it cannot substantiate a general state-of-the-art claim.

Statistical evidence is inadequate. Atari reports averages over five seeds without per-game uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests; Hollow Knight uses only three seeds; and several appendix ablations do not clearly report seed counts. Selecting the best of multiple feature extractors and representations further increases the need for uncertainty-aware comparisons.

The Atari gains are inconsistent and partially driven by large-score games: OC-STORM's median improvement over its STORM baseline is much smaller than its mean improvement, and it substantially degrades several games. The post-hoc split into 'object-detectable' games lacks a quantitative detection criterion and risks selection bias.

The custom Hollow Knight evidence is weak and difficult to reproduce. The environment depends on a bespoke Windows virtual-machine wrapper, game mod, manually configured bosses, charms, object annotations, reward design, and pseudo-termination scheme. No complete artifact or working project-page link is provided, and the comparison is mainly against one baseline under this new setup.

The method is incremental relative to FOCUS and prior object-centric world models: its main change is replacing masks with internal features from pretrained video segmentation and adding object tokens. The paper does not establish that the proposed spatial-temporal architecture, rather than privileged semantic supervision or extra capacity, is responsible for the improvements.

The robustness analysis trains and evaluates under matched random feature zeroing, which does not represent structured, temporally correlated tracking failures. It therefore does not justify robustness to realistic segmentation errors. Segmentation quality itself is never quantitatively measured.

The central motivation—that pixel reconstruction neglects task-critical objects—is supported mainly by a qualitative reconstruction example. There is no systematic analysis of object-level reconstruction, latent prediction, imagined-rollout accuracy, or their relationship to control performance.

The formal presentation contains consequential ambiguities and errors. In particular, the termination term in Equation 5 has the wrong sign for a minimized binary cross-entropy loss, while other equations use inconsistent state notation. Without released implementation, it is impossible to determine whether these are typographical errors or defects in the actual training objective.

The annotation burden and prior task knowledge are understated: the user must choose the number and identities of relevant objects separately for every game or boss and label multiple masks. Annotation time, annotator protocol, object-selection sensitivity, and performance with imperfectly chosen objects are not adequately characterized.

strengths: OC-STORM addresses an important limitation of pixel-reconstruction world models: small, decision-relevant entities can be overwhelmed by complex backgrounds. Using compact features from pretrained video-segmentation models is intuitive and practically relevant.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad, covering all 26 Atari 100k games, six Hollow Knight bosses, four Meta-World tasks, two world-model backbones, two segmentation models, and both vector- and mask-based object representations.

The controlled Atari comparisons provide convincing positive evidence. Cutie-OC improves STORM from 114.2% to 134.8% mean human-normalized score and from 42.5% to 43.8% median, while the object-detectable subset improves particularly strongly from 147.7% to 186.2%. Improvements also transfer to the DreamerV3 backbone.

The Hollow Knight experiments are a valuable contribution because they test visually rich, dynamic environments where the motivating failure mode is substantially more realistic than in standard Atari games. OC-STORM generally learns faster and performs better than matched STORM runs.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses of segmentation failures, annotation count, missing objects, object-only versus combined inputs, policy architecture, computational overhead, and feature completeness. These investigations support the proposed design and expose meaningful limitations.

The method retains raw visual inputs alongside object features, making it reasonably robust when object detection is incomplete or when geometric scene information is difficult to represent as discrete objects.
The presentation is generally clear, the architecture and hyperparameters are documented, and computational costs are reported.
weaknesses: The core novelty is moderate: the work primarily integrates pretrained segmentation features into established STORM/Dreamer machinery. It does not introduce a fundamentally new object-learning objective, segmentation method, or model-based RL algorithm.

The strongest comparisons do not fully isolate the source of improvement. OC-STORM receives pretrained, manually supervised semantic information and adds object tokens and model capacity, but there is no parameter- or compute-matched baseline using simpler privileged features such as boxes, centroids, crops, or generic pretrained visual tokens. Thus, the evidence does not establish that the particular object-centric architecture is necessary.

Uncertainty reporting is insufficient for several central claims. Atari tables contain means over five seeds but no standard errors, confidence intervals, or significance tests, while Hollow Knight uses only three seeds. Some reported gains are modest or inconsistent—for example, God Tamer return improves while win rate decreases—and Pure Vessel remains unsolved at 100k steps.

The claim of state-of-the-art sample efficiency on Hollow Knight is too strong because this is not a standardized benchmark, the environment wrapper and reward shaping differ from prior work, and the only external comparison is explicitly acknowledged as not strictly fair. On Atari, OC-STORM is also below several published methods in mean or median aggregate performance.

The object selection and annotation procedure injects task knowledge and scales with the number of environments and objects. Six annotated frames per Atari game and twelve per Hollow Knight boss are manageable, but the paper does not quantify annotation time, sensitivity to annotator choices, or performance with automatically selected objects.

Reproducibility is limited: the displayed project-page field is blank, no code or annotation release is identified, and the custom Hollow Knight setup depends on a proprietary game, a bespoke mod, virtual-machine infrastructure, and nonstandard rewards. Important details about preprocessing and replay-time handling of the stateful tracker could also be clearer.

The mask baseline is described as a FOCUS-like reimplementation rather than a faithful reproduction, so conclusions that vector representations outperform prior mask-based object-centric methods should be stated more cautiously.

There are technical and editorial ambiguities. In Equation 5 the stated binary cross-entropy termination term has the wrong sign if the total objective is minimized, and modality-specific reconstruction-loss weighting is not specified despite the very different dimensionalities of pixel and object-feature targets.

The method assumes a fixed, user-specified number and identity of objects and inherits tracker failures for duplicated, occluded, newly appearing, or deformable entities. These limitations restrict applicability to open-ended environments despite the fallback visual stream.
